Continue
kŏn-tĭn´ū
v.i. (to remain, persist, abide; rendering Greek menō, epimenō, proskartereō)
From Latin continuare, to join without break. In the New Testament continuance is the ordinary test of reality — not how a profession began, but whether it lasted.

Biblical Definition

To continue is to remain in a thing without break, and the New Testament makes it the standing evidence of genuine faith. Our Lord said it to men who had just believed on Him: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) — discipleship proved by remaining, not by the initial response. Paul says the same of the whole gospel hope: reconciliation is presented to God “if ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel” (Col 1:23). The Jerusalem church shows what continuance looks like in practice, and it is unspectacular: “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — four things, done again and again. And Paul forecloses the abuse of the doctrine of grace with the same verb: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” (Rom 6:1). One kind of continuing proves life; the other proves its absence.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines continue as to remain in a state or place, to last, to persevere, to be steadfast or constant in any course.

expand to see more

CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely.

2. To last; to be durable; to endure; to be permanent.

3. To persevere; to be steadfast or constant in any course.

CONTINUE, v.t. To protract; not to cease from or to terminate.

2. To extend from one thing to another; to produce or draw out in length.

Key Scripture

Joh 8:31 — "Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;"

Col 1:23 — "If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;"

Act 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Rom 6:1 — "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?"

Modern Corruption

Continuance has been made optional by a doctrine of bare decisionism, in which a past profession settles the matter and perseverance is treated as an extra for the keen.

expand to see more

The dictionary holds the perseverance of the saints, and precisely for that reason it will not accept the counterfeit that goes by the same territory. Bare once saved always saved treats a recorded decision as the whole of the question and makes continuing irrelevant; the Confession, with Scripture, teaches that those whom God has accepted in the Beloved can neither totally nor finally fall away, and that this shows itself in their continuing. John 8:31 and Colossians 1:23 are not threats to assurance but its instruments: the man who continues has the evidence in hand.

Acts 2:42 keeps the doctrine from becoming abstract, and the list is deliberately ordinary — doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers. Perseverance is not a heroic posture maintained under floodlights; it is showing up, hearing the Word, taking the Supper, and praying, for decades. Romans 6:1 then closes the other door. The grace that guarantees continuance in Christ is the same grace that makes continuance in sin unthinkable, and Paul's answer to the question is God forbid.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek menō (G3306), to abide or remain, epimenō (G1961), to continue in, and proskartereō (G4342), to persist steadfastly — the evidence of a real work.

expand to see more

Greek menō (G3306) — to abide, remain, continue; “if ye continue in my word” (Joh 8:31), and the abiding of Joh 15.

Greek epimenō (G1961) — to remain in, persist; “if ye continue in the faith” (Col 1:23), and “shall we continue in sin” (Rom 6:1).

Greek proskartereō (G4342) — to attend constantly, persevere; the fourfold continuance of Act 2:42.

Usage

"“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” — the test is remaining."

"“They continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” — four ordinary things, repeated."

"“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” — the other continuance, forbidden."
